A **5–10 minute exploration**, using a prediction before each control change. The diagram and result update locally; no network service is used.

### Predict first

If only neutral HA enters the organic phase, will raising aqueous pH increase or decrease the total solute recovered there? What extra information beyond pH and pKa must the model use?

### Explore

1. Keep P = 10 and equal 50 mL phases. Compare the mostly neutral and mostly ionised acid presets. Explain why aqueous deprotonation changes the effective distribution ratio D.

2. Hold the aqueous pH fixed. Double the organic-phase volume, then double the aqueous-phase volume instead. Predict the direction of organic recovery before each change.

3. Change P while holding pH and volumes fixed. State which property P represents and why changing P is not the same operation as changing acid strength. Reset and compare all three total-solute fractions.

### Take-away

Explain why an aqueous ionisation curve alone cannot predict extraction. Which additional assumptions would fail if ion pairing carried A⁻ into the organic phase?

### Model and limits

Teaching extension: only neutral HA partitions, with P = [HA]organic/[HA]aqueous; A⁻ stays in water. Aqueous pH is externally fixed, equilibrium is reached, volumes remain constant and phases are immiscible. D = P/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)); organic fraction = D Vorg/(Vaq + D Vorg). Both volumes use the same units. The equal-height layer drawing is schematic; layer order does not predict solvent density. This is not an experimental extraction protocol.
